L02 · Matrices & Linear Systems

L02 · Matrices — Operations, Inverses and Linear Equations

Lecture 2 (slides "Matrices – Operations, Inverses and Linear Equations", 49 pages) · Boyd & Vandenberghe Ch. 6, 8, 10, 11 · Deisenroth Ch. 2

Lecture 2 slides (PDF) Revision notes: Matrices via traffic networks Problem Set 3 PSet 3 solutions Tutorial 1 (Gram matrix, 3-D least squares)

What this lecture covers, in order: matrix notation and special matrices → applications → addition, scaling, transpose, symmetric/skew-symmetric, Frobenius norm, trace → matrix–vector product (row view, column view, linear-map view) and its applications → matrix–matrix product, outer product, Gram matrix → systems of linear equations → left inverse, right inverse, inverse → special invertible matrices (diagonal, Vandermonde, Gram, orthogonal) → pseudo-inverses. Plus, from the outline/revision notes: determinant as area scaling and the standard geometric transformations.

Intuition: Running problem

Lahore's traffic hub watches 3 intersections × 4 approaches. Stack the three queue vectors as rows:
A=(30182512221015840253020)∈R3×4.A=\begin{pmatrix}30&18&25&12\\22&10&15&8\\40&25&30&20\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times4}.A=​302240​181025​251530​12820​​∈R3×4.
A row is one intersection (all approaches); a column is one approach across intersections (column 3 = southbound (25,15,30)(25,15,30)(25,15,30)). One index is no longer enough: "15" is A23A_{23}A23​.

#1. Matrices: definition and notation

Definition: Matrix

A matrix is a two-dimensional array of numbers (a "2-D vector"), written with a capital letter in square or round brackets:
A=[−1.117.32.730.119.18.4](2×3).A=\begin{bmatrix}-1.1&17.3&2.7\\30.1&19.1&8.4\end{bmatrix}\quad(2\times3).A=[−1.130.1​17.319.1​2.78.4​](2×3).
Size: mmm rows × nnn columns, written B∈Rm×nB\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}B∈Rm×n ("an m×nm\times nm×n matrix"). Entry BijB_{ij}Bij​ = row iii, column jjj; above, A21=30.1A_{21}=30.1A21​=30.1.

A matrix can be read as a stack of column vectors A=[a1 a2 ⋯ an]A=[a_1\ a_2\ \cdots\ a_n]A=[a1​ a2​ ⋯ an​], aj∈Rma_j\in\mathbb{R}^maj​∈Rm, or a stack of row vectors.

#Special matrices

Name Definition
Square / tall / wide m=nm=nm=n / m>nm>nm>n / m<nm<nm<n
Zero matrix 0∈Rm×n0\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}0∈Rm×n all entries 0
Identity I=In∈Rn×nI=I_n\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}I=In​∈Rn×n (I)ij=δij(I)_{ij}=\delta_{ij}(I)ij​=δij​: ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere
Diagonal square, all off-diagonal entries 0: diag⁡(d1,…,dn)\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_n)diag(d1​,…,dn​)
Upper / lower triangular zeros below / above the diagonal, e.g. [1−10.701.2−1.1003.2]\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&0.7\\0&1.2&-1.1\\0&0&3.2\end{bmatrix}​100​−11.20​0.7−1.13.2​​, [−0.60−0.33.5]\begin{bmatrix}-0.6&0\\-0.3&3.5\end{bmatrix}[−0.6−0.3​03.5​]
Block matrix built from sub-matrices, A=[BCDE]A=\begin{bmatrix}B&C\\D&E\end{bmatrix}A=[BD​CE​] (blocks in a row share row-count, blocks in a column share column-count)
Symmetric / skew-symmetric A=A⊤A=A^\topA=A⊤ / A=−A⊤A=-A^\topA=−A⊤ (§3)
Orthogonal square with orthonormal columns, Q⊤Q=IQ^\top Q=IQ⊤Q=I (§10)
Permutation one 1 in every row and every column, zeros elsewhere (§5)

#Applications (slides p5–6)

  • RGB image: each colour channel is an m×nm\times nm×n matrix of pixel intensities (three matrices for one image).
  • Quantities: A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n = amounts of nnn products held/produced/required at mmm locations or by mmm customers — e.g. nnn products in mmm warehouses.
  • Time series grouped over time: a 12×2012\times2012×20 matrix of monthly temperature/rainfall/pressure for 20 cities of Pakistan; a 30×730\times730×7 matrix of patients over the next 30 days for 7 states/territories; exchange rates; audio.
  • Data matrix / feature matrix X∈Rm×nX\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}X∈Rm×n: row iii = sample iii's features, column jjj = feature jjj across samples.
Remember

A matrix is an m×nm\times nm×n grid; read it as columns, as rows, or (soon) as a machine that maps Rn→Rm\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^mRn→Rm.

#2. Addition and scaling

Definition

For A,BA,BA,B of the same size: (A+B)ij=Aij+Bij(A+B)_{ij}=A_{ij}+B_{ij}(A+B)ij​=Aij​+Bij​. For scalar α\alphaα: (αA)ij=αAij(\alpha A)_{ij}=\alpha A_{ij}(αA)ij​=αAij​.

Slide examples:
[047031]+[122304]=[169335],(−2)[169360]=[−2−12−18−6−120].\begin{bmatrix}0&4\\7&0\\3&1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&3\\0&4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&6\\9&3\\3&5\end{bmatrix},\qquad (-2)\begin{bmatrix}1&6\\9&3\\6&0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2&-12\\-18&-6\\-12&0\end{bmatrix}.​073​401​​+​120​234​​=​193​635​​,(−2)​196​630​​=​−2−18−12​−12−60​​.

Traffic: with change matrix B=(4−3−5212−10−243−1)B=\begin{pmatrix}4&-3&-5&2\\1&2&-1&0\\-2&4&3&-1\end{pmatrix}B=​41−2​−324​−5−13​20−1​​, A+B=(34152014231214838293319)A+B=\begin{pmatrix}34&15&20&14\\23&12&14&8\\38&29&33&19\end{pmatrix}A+B=​342338​151229​201433​14819​​ updates the whole city at once; a uniform 10% rise in traffic is 1.1A1.1A1.1A.

Remember

Add and scale entry-wise; addition needs identical sizes.

#3. Transpose, symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices

Definition: Transpose

A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n ⇒ A⊤∈Rn×mA^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}A⊤∈Rn×m with (A⊤)ij=Aji(A^\top)_{ij}=A_{ji}(A⊤)ij​=Aji​: rows become columns.
[047031]⊤=[073401].\begin{bmatrix}0&4\\7&0\\3&1\end{bmatrix}^\top=\begin{bmatrix}0&7&3\\4&0&1\end{bmatrix}.​073​401​​⊤=[04​70​31​].

Rules: (A⊤)⊤=A(A^\top)^\top=A(A⊤)⊤=A, (A+B)⊤=A⊤+B⊤(A+B)^\top=A^\top+B^\top(A+B)⊤=A⊤+B⊤, (αA)⊤=αA⊤(\alpha A)^\top=\alpha A^\top(αA)⊤=αA⊤, (AB)⊤=B⊤A⊤(AB)^\top=B^\top A^\top(AB)⊤=B⊤A⊤ (order reverses; so (ABC)⊤=C⊤B⊤A⊤(ABC)^\top=C^\top B^\top A^\top(ABC)⊤=C⊤B⊤A⊤, not A⊤B⊤C⊤A^\top B^\top C^\topA⊤B⊤C⊤).

Definition: Symmetric and skew-symmetric

Square AAA is symmetric if A=A⊤A=A^\topA=A⊤ (Aij=AjiA_{ij}=A_{ji}Aij​=Aji​, mirror image across the main diagonal).
Square AAA is skew-symmetric if A=−A⊤A=-A^\topA=−A⊤ (Aij=−AjiA_{ij}=-A_{ji}Aij​=−Aji​); then Aii=−AiiA_{ii}=-A_{ii}Aii​=−Aii​ forces all diagonal entries to be 0.

Examples from the revision notes: a pairwise "compatibility" matrix between approaches is naturally symmetric; a net-flow matrix (flow i→ji\to ji→j = −flow j→ij\to ij→i) is naturally skew-symmetric, e.g. (06−2−6032−30)\begin{pmatrix}0&6&-2\\-6&0&3\\2&-3&0\end{pmatrix}​0−62​60−3​−230​​.

Theorem / Key result: Symmetric + skew-symmetric decomposition

Every square matrix splits uniquely as
A=S+K,S=A+A⊤2 (symmetric part),K=A−A⊤2 (skew-symmetric part).A=S+K,\qquad S=\frac{A+A^\top}{2}\ (\text{symmetric part}),\qquad K=\frac{A-A^\top}{2}\ (\text{skew-symmetric part}).A=S+K,S=2A+A⊤​ (symmetric part),K=2A−A⊤​ (skew-symmetric part).
Check: S⊤=A⊤+A2=SS^\top=\frac{A^\top+A}{2}=SS⊤=2A⊤+A​=S, K⊤=A⊤−A2=−KK^\top=\frac{A^\top-A}{2}=-KK⊤=2A⊤−A​=−K, S+K=AS+K=AS+K=A.

Worked example: 2026 Quiz 3, Q1

A=(4202)A=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\0&2\end{pmatrix}A=(40​22​), A⊤=(4022)A^\top=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\2&2\end{pmatrix}A⊤=(42​02​), so S=(4112)S=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}S=(41​12​), K=(01−10)K=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}K=(0−1​10​).

Worked example: PSet 3, P2

A=(2−10134−205)A=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\1&3&4\\-2&0&5\end{pmatrix}A=​21−2​−130​045​​: S=(20−1032−125)S=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&-1\\0&3&2\\-1&2&5\end{pmatrix}S=​20−1​032​−125​​, K=(0−11102−1−20)K=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&1\\1&0&2\\-1&-2&0\end{pmatrix}K=​01−1​−10−2​120​​. Since S≠0S\neq0S=0 and K≠0K\neq0K=0, AAA is neither symmetric nor skew-symmetric.

Facts (PSet 3 P3): AAA symmetric ⇒ A2A^2A2 symmetric (always: (AA)⊤=A⊤A⊤=AA(AA)^\top=A^\top A^\top=AA(AA)⊤=A⊤A⊤=AA); A,BA,BA,B symmetric ⇒ ABABAB symmetric only sometimes (iff AB=BAAB=BAAB=BA; e.g. A=(1000)A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}A=(10​00​), B=(0110)B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}B=(01​10​) gives AB=(0100)AB=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}AB=(00​10​), not symmetric); sum of symmetric matrices is symmetric; A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A and AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ are always symmetric.

Remember

A⊤A^\topA⊤ swaps rows and columns, (AB)⊤=B⊤A⊤(AB)^\top=B^\top A^\top(AB)⊤=B⊤A⊤; every square matrix =12(A+A⊤)+12(A−A⊤)=\tfrac12(A+A^\top)+\tfrac12(A-A^\top)=21​(A+A⊤)+21​(A−A⊤).

#4. Frobenius norm and trace

Definition: Frobenius norm

∥A∥F=∑i=1m∑j=1n∣Aij∣2\|A\|_F=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n |A_{ij}|^2}∥A∥F​=i=1∑m​j=1∑n​∣Aij​∣2​
= the 2-norm of the vector obtained by stacking all entries of AAA.

Uses (slides): error of a matrix approximation, ∥A−A^∥F\|A-\hat A\|_F∥A−A^∥F​ (e.g. low-rank compression); regularization — adding ∥W∥F2\|W\|_F^2∥W∥F2​ to a loss penalises large weights and fights overfitting. It inherits the norm rules: ∥2A∥F=2∥A∥F\|2A\|_F=2\|A\|_F∥2A∥F​=2∥A∥F​.

Examples: ∥(1234)∥F=1+4+9+16=30≈5.48\left\|\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}\right\|_F=\sqrt{1+4+9+16}=\sqrt{30}\approx5.48​(13​24​)​F​=1+4+9+16​=30​≈5.48 (2024 Mid); ∥(0523)∥F=0+25+4+9=38\left\|\begin{pmatrix}0&5\\2&3\end{pmatrix}\right\|_F=\sqrt{0+25+4+9}=\sqrt{38}​(02​53​)​F​=0+25+4+9​=38​ (2025 Mid); PSet 3: ∥A∥F=1+4+9+0+16+1=31\|A\|_F=\sqrt{1+4+9+0+16+1}=\sqrt{31}∥A∥F​=1+4+9+0+16+1​=31​; traffic change matrix ∥B∥F=74≈8.6\|B\|_F=\sqrt{74}\approx8.6∥B∥F​=74​≈8.6.

Definition: Trace

For square A∈Rn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}A∈Rn×n: tr⁡(A)=∑i=1nAii\operatorname{tr}(A)=\sum_{i=1}^n A_{ii}tr(A)=∑i=1n​Aii​ (sum of diagonal entries). Undefined for non-square matrices.

Properties:

  • Linear: tr⁡(A+B)=tr⁡A+tr⁡B\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}A+\operatorname{tr}Btr(A+B)=trA+trB, tr⁡(αA)=αtr⁡A\operatorname{tr}(\alpha A)=\alpha\operatorname{tr}Atr(αA)=αtrA; tr⁡(A⊤)=tr⁡A\operatorname{tr}(A^\top)=\operatorname{tr}Atr(A⊤)=trA; tr⁡(In)=n\operatorname{tr}(I_n)=ntr(In​)=n.
  • Cyclic invariance: tr⁡(ABC)=tr⁡(CAB)=tr⁡(BCA)\operatorname{tr}(ABC)=\operatorname{tr}(CAB)=\operatorname{tr}(BCA)tr(ABC)=tr(CAB)=tr(BCA); in particular tr⁡(AB)=tr⁡(BA)\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)tr(AB)=tr(BA).
  • But tr⁡(AB)≠tr⁡(A)tr⁡(B)\operatorname{tr}(AB)\neq\operatorname{tr}(A)\operatorname{tr}(B)tr(AB)=tr(A)tr(B) in general (A=B=I2A=B=I_2A=B=I2​: 2≠42\neq42=4).
  • Link to Frobenius: ∥A∥F2=tr⁡(A⊤A)=tr⁡(AA⊤)\|A\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}(A^\top A)=\operatorname{tr}(AA^\top)∥A∥F2​=tr(A⊤A)=tr(AA⊤) (the diagonal of A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A holds the squared column norms). Traffic: tr⁡(AA⊤)=2023+873+3525=6421=302+182+⋯+202\operatorname{tr}(AA^\top)=2023+873+3525=6421=30^2+18^2+\dots+20^2tr(AA⊤)=2023+873+3525=6421=302+182+⋯+202.
  • Use in PCA: if Λ\LambdaΛ is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues of a covariance matrix, tr⁡(Λ)\operatorname{tr}(\Lambda)tr(Λ) = total variance; the fraction kept by chosen components guides how many to keep. Also tr⁡(A)=∑iλi\operatorname{tr}(A)=\sum_i\lambda_itr(A)=∑i​λi​ (L06).
Remember

∥A∥F\|A\|_F∥A∥F​ = Euclidean length of all entries, ∥A∥F2=tr⁡(A⊤A)\|A\|_F^2=\operatorname{tr}(A^\top A)∥A∥F2​=tr(A⊤A); trace = diagonal sum, linear and cyclic.

#5. Matrix–vector multiplication

Definition

A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n, x∈Rnx\in\mathbb{R}^nx∈Rn (number of columns of AAA = size of xxx). Then y=Ax∈Rmy=Ax\in\mathbb{R}^my=Ax∈Rm with
yi=∑k=1nAikxk=Ai1x1+⋯+Ainxn,i=1,…,m.y_i=\sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik}x_k=A_{i1}x_1+\dots+A_{in}x_n,\qquad i=1,\dots,m .yi​=k=1∑n​Aik​xk​=Ai1​x1​+⋯+Ain​xn​,i=1,…,m.

Slide example:
[02−1−211][21−1]=[(0)(2)+(2)(1)+(−1)(−1)(−2)(2)+(1)(1)+(1)(−1)]=[3−4].\begin{bmatrix}0&2&-1\\-2&1&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\\-1\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}(0)(2)+(2)(1)+(-1)(-1)\\(-2)(2)+(1)(1)+(1)(-1)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\-4\end{bmatrix}.[0−2​21​−11​]​21−1​​=[(0)(2)+(2)(1)+(−1)(−1)(−2)(2)+(1)(1)+(1)(−1)​]=[3−4​].

#Three interpretations

(1) Rows — inner products. With rows r1⊤,…,rm⊤r_1^\top,\dots,r_m^\topr1⊤​,…,rm⊤​ of AAA: yi=ri⊤xy_i=r_i^\top xyi​=ri⊤​x. Each output is a score of xxx against one row. Traffic: A1=(85,55,115)A\mathbf 1=(85,55,115)A1=(85,55,115) = total cars at each intersection.

(2) Columns — linear combination. With columns a1,…,ana_1,\dots,a_na1​,…,an​:
y=Ax=x1a1+x2a2+⋯+xnan.y=Ax=x_1a_1+x_2a_2+\dots+x_na_n .y=Ax=x1​a1​+x2​a2​+⋯+xn​an​.
AxAxAx is a linear combination of the columns of AAA; the coefficients are the entries of xxx. Consequences: Aej=ajAe_j=a_jAej​=aj​ (picks column jjj); the set of all AxAxAx is the span of the columns — the column space (L03).

A=(2−1314−2051)A=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&3\\1&4&-2\\0&5&1\end{pmatrix}A=​210​−145​3−21​​, b=(738)b=\begin{pmatrix}7\\3\\8\end{pmatrix}b=​738​​:
Ab=7(210)+3(−145)+8(3−21)=(35323).Ab=7\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}+3\begin{pmatrix}-1\\4\\5\end{pmatrix}+8\begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}35\\3\\23\end{pmatrix}.Ab=7​210​​+3​−145​​+8​3−21​​=​35323​​.

(3) Linear transformation / input–output system. x∈Rn→A→y∈Rmx\in\mathbb{R}^n\to\boxed{A}\to y\in\mathbb{R}^mx∈Rn→A​→y∈Rm. The map f(x)=Axf(x)=Axf(x)=Ax is linear: A(x+x′)=Ax+Ax′A(x+x')=Ax+Ax'A(x+x′)=Ax+Ax′ and A(αx)=αAxA(\alpha x)=\alpha AxA(αx)=αAx (PSet 3 P13 checks this numerically).

#Applications of y=Axy=Axy=Ax (slides p18–23)

With A∈R200×70A\in\mathbb{R}^{200\times70}A∈R200×70 = quantity of 70 products in 200 warehouses:

  • Total value of stock per warehouse: price vector p∈R70p\in\mathbb{R}^{70}p∈R70 ⇒ y=Ap∈R200y=Ap\in\mathbb{R}^{200}y=Ap∈R200.
  • Total weight per warehouse: y=Awy=Awy=Aw with per-unit weights www (logistics planning).
  • Seasonal/discounted pricing: y=Apseasony=Ap_{\text{season}}y=Apseason​.
  • Replenishment demand: replenishment coefficients rrr ⇒ y=Ary=Ary=Ar.

PSet 3 P5: Q=(1005246080371)Q=\begin{pmatrix}10&0&5&2\\4&6&0&8\\0&3&7&1\end{pmatrix}Q=​1040​063​507​281​​, p=(5,10,2,7)p=(5,10,2,7)p=(5,10,2,7) ⇒ Qp=(74,136,51)Qp=(74,136,51)Qp=(74,136,51) = stock value at each warehouse; Q⊤e1=(10,0,5,2)Q^\top e_1=(10,0,5,2)Q⊤e1​=(10,0,5,2) = products held at warehouse 1.

With feature matrix A∈Rd×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}A∈Rd×n (each column a ddd-dim feature vector of one image):

  • Classification scores: weight vector w∈Rdw\in\mathbb{R}^dw∈Rd ⇒ y=A⊤w∈Rny=A^\top w\in\mathbb{R}^ny=A⊤w∈Rn, one score per image.
  • Similarity to a reference image qqq: y=A⊤qy=A^\top qy=A⊤q — entry jjj is the dot product (or cosine similarity if normalised) of image jjj with qqq; used in image retrieval and recommendation.

#6. Matrix–matrix multiplication

Definition

A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n, B∈Rn×pB\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}B∈Rn×p (columns of AAA = rows of BBB = nnn). Then C=AB∈Rm×pC=AB\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}C=AB∈Rm×p with
Cij=∑k=1nAikBkj=Ai1B1j+⋯+AinBnj,C_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^n A_{ik}B_{kj}=A_{i1}B_{1j}+\dots+A_{in}B_{nj},Cij​=k=1∑n​Aik​Bkj​=Ai1​B1j​+⋯+Ain​Bnj​,
i.e. CijC_{ij}Cij​ = (row iii of AAA)·(column jjj of BBB). Dimension rule: (m×n)(n×p)=(m×p)(m\times n)(n\times p)=(m\times p)(m×n)(n×p)=(m×p).

Column view: AB=[Ab1 Ab2 ⋯ Abp]AB=[Ab_1\ Ab_2\ \cdots\ Ab_p]AB=[Ab1​ Ab2​ ⋯ Abp​] — each column of ABABAB is AAA times a column of BBB.

Properties:

  • Not commutative: AB≠BAAB\neq BAAB=BA in general (PSet 3 P7: A=(1201)A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}A=(10​21​), B=(0110)B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}B=(01​10​) give AB=(2110)AB=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}AB=(21​10​), BA=(0112)BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}BA=(01​12​)). Often only one order is even defined.
  • Associative: (AB)C=A(BC)(AB)C=A(BC)(AB)C=A(BC), so we write ABCABCABC. Scalars move freely: (γA)B=γ(AB)=A(γB)(\gamma A)B=\gamma(AB)=A(\gamma B)(γA)B=γ(AB)=A(γB).
  • Distributive: A(B+C)=AB+ACA(B+C)=AB+ACA(B+C)=AB+AC.
  • Transpose: (AB)⊤=B⊤A⊤(AB)^\top=B^\top A^\top(AB)⊤=B⊤A⊤.
  • Block multiplication (dimensions compatible): [ABCD][WYXZ]=[AW+BXAY+BZCW+DXCY+DZ]\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}W&Y\\X&Z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}AW+BX&AY+BZ\\CW+DX&CY+DZ\end{bmatrix}[AC​BD​][WX​YZ​]=[AW+BXCW+DX​AY+BZCY+DZ​].
  • AI=IA=AAI=IA=AAI=IA=A.
Definition: Outer product

For a∈Rma\in\mathbb{R}^ma∈Rm, b∈Rnb\in\mathbb{R}^nb∈Rn: ab⊤∈Rm×nab^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}ab⊤∈Rm×n with entries aibja_ib_jai​bj​:
ab⊤=[a1b1a1b2⋯a1bn⋮⋮amb1amb2⋯ambn].ab^\top=\begin{bmatrix}a_1b_1&a_1b_2&\cdots&a_1b_n\\ \vdots&&&\vdots\\ a_mb_1&a_mb_2&\cdots&a_mb_n\end{bmatrix}.ab⊤=​a1​b1​⋮am​b1​​a1​b2​am​b2​​⋯⋯​a1​bn​⋮am​bn​​​.
Every row is a multiple of b⊤b^\topb⊤ and every column a multiple of aaa, so a non-zero outer product has rank 1.

Definition: Gram matrix

For A=[a1 ⋯ an]A=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_n]A=[a1​ ⋯ an​]:
G=A⊤A=[a1⊤a1a1⊤a2⋯a1⊤an⋮⋱⋮an⊤a1an⊤a2⋯an⊤an],Gij=ai⊤aj.G=A^\top A=\begin{bmatrix}a_1^\top a_1&a_1^\top a_2&\cdots&a_1^\top a_n\\ \vdots&&\ddots&\vdots\\ a_n^\top a_1&a_n^\top a_2&\cdots&a_n^\top a_n\end{bmatrix},\qquad G_{ij}=a_i^\top a_j .G=A⊤A=​a1⊤​a1​⋮an⊤​a1​​a1⊤​a2​an⊤​a2​​⋯⋱⋯​a1⊤​an​⋮an⊤​an​​​,Gij​=ai⊤​aj​.

#7. Systems of linear equations

Definition: Formulation

A11x1+A12x2+⋯+A1nxn=b1  ⋮Am1x1+Am2x2+⋯+Amnxn=bm⟺[A11⋯A1n⋮⋱⋮Am1⋯Amn]⏟A∈Rm×n[x1⋮xn]⏟x∈Rn=[b1⋮bm]⏟b∈Rm\begin{aligned}A_{11}x_1+A_{12}x_2+\dots+A_{1n}x_n&=b_1\\ &\ \,\vdots\\ A_{m1}x_1+A_{m2}x_2+\dots+A_{mn}x_n&=b_m\end{aligned} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}A_{11}&\cdots&A_{1n}\\ \vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ A_{m1}&\cdots&A_{mn}\end{bmatrix}}_{A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\ \vdots\\ x_n\end{bmatrix}}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}b_1\\ \vdots\\ b_m\end{bmatrix}}_{b\in\mathbb{R}^m}A11​x1​+A12​x2​+⋯+A1n​xn​Am1​x1​+Am2​x2​+⋯+Amn​xn​​=b1​ ⋮=bm​​⟺A∈Rm×n​A11​⋮Am1​​⋯⋱⋯​A1n​⋮Amn​​​​​x∈Rn​x1​⋮xn​​​​​=b∈Rm​b1​⋮bm​​​​​
x1,…,xnx_1,\dots,x_nx1​,…,xn​: variables/unknowns. b1,…,bmb_1,\dots,b_mb1​,…,bm​: knowns, measurements, right-hand side. AijA_{ij}Aij​: coefficient of variable jjj in equation iii.

Three possible outcomes: one solution, multiple (infinitely many) solutions, or no solution.

Shape Name Meaning
m<nm<nm<n under-determined fewer equations than unknowns (wide AAA)
m=nm=nm=n square
m>nm>nm>n over-determined more equations than unknowns (tall AAA)

The shape alone does not decide the outcome — always check.

A=[11101−1]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&0\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}A=​111​10−1​​, b=[1−10]b=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\\0\end{bmatrix}b=​1−10​​. Rows 2–3 force x=(−1,−1)x=(-1,-1)x=(−1,−1), but then row 1 gives −2≠1-2\neq1−2=1 ⇒ no solution.

Both x=[102]x=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{bmatrix}x=​102​​ and x=[011]x=\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}x=​011​​ work — infinitely many solutions.

Ax=bAx=bAx=b asks "which combination of the columns of AAA gives bbb?"; tall = over-determined, wide = under-determined, but only consistency decides none/one/many.

#8. Left inverse

Definition

XXX is a left inverse of AAA if XA=IXA=IXA=I. AAA is left-invertible if it has at least one left inverse. (A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n ⇒ X∈Rn×mX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}X∈Rn×m, I=InI=I_nI=In​.)

Slide example: A=[−3−44611]A=\begin{bmatrix}-3&-4\\4&6\\1&1\end{bmatrix}A=​−341​−461​​ has (at least) two left inverses,
X1=19[−11−101678−11],X2=[0−1/2301/2−2].X_1=\frac19\begin{bmatrix}-11&-10&16\\7&8&-11\end{bmatrix},\qquad X_2=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1/2&3\\0&1/2&-2\end{bmatrix}.X1​=91​[−117​−108​16−11​],X2​=[00​−1/21/2​3−2​].
Check one entry: row 1 of X1X_1X1​ times column 1 of AAA =19(33−40+16)=1=\tfrac19(33-40+16)=1=91​(33−40+16)=1. A left inverse need not be unique.

Theorem / Key result: Left-invertible ⇒ columns linearly independent
Derivation

Suppose XA=IXA=IXA=I and Ax=0Ax=0Ax=0. Then x=Ix=(XA)x=X(Ax)=X0=0x=Ix=(XA)x=X(Ax)=X0=0x=Ix=(XA)x=X(Ax)=X0=0. So Ax=0Ax=0Ax=0 only for x=0x=0x=0 — the columns are independent.

Connect with the independence–dimension inequality: if AAA is wide (m<nm<nm<n), its nnn columns live in Rm\mathbb{R}^mRm and must be dependent, so a wide matrix is never left-invertible. Left-invertible matrices are square or tall (m≥nm\ge nm≥n). (Quiz 4: "a wide matrix can have a left inverse" — False; e.g. (1 0)(1\ 0)(1 0).)

Connection with Ax=bAx=bAx=b (AAA square or over-determined). If XA=IXA=IXA=I, multiply Ax=bAx=bAx=b by XXX: x=Xbx=Xbx=Xb.

  • If a solution exists, x=Xbx=Xbx=Xb is the only one — at most one solution (Quiz 4 b proof: two solutions x,x~x,\tilde xx,x~ both equal CbCbCb).
  • If no solution exists, x=Xbx=Xbx=Xb will not satisfy Ax=bAx=bAx=b — so compute XbXbXb and check A(Xb)=bA(Xb)=bA(Xb)=b.

So a left inverse tells you whether an over-determined system is solvable and, if so, gives the unique solution.

Remember

XA=IXA=IXA=I: possible only for tall/square AAA with independent columns; it gives at most one solution x=Xbx=Xbx=Xb — verify it.

#9. Right inverse

Definition

XXX is a right inverse of AAA if AX=IAX=IAX=I (I=ImI=I_mI=Im​). AAA is right-invertible if it has at least one.

Slide example: A=[101011]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}A=[10​01​11​] has right inverses
12[1−1−1111],[100100],[1−10001].\frac12\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\0&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.21​​1−11​−111​​,​100​010​​,​100​−101​​.

Connection with the left inverse: if AX=IAX=IAX=I then I=I⊤=(AX)⊤=X⊤A⊤I=I^\top=(AX)^\top=X^\top A^\topI=I⊤=(AX)⊤=X⊤A⊤, so X⊤X^\topX⊤ is a left inverse of A⊤A^\topA⊤. Hence: right-invertible ⇔ A⊤A^\topA⊤ left-invertible ⇔ columns of A⊤A^\topA⊤ independent ⇔ rows of AAA independent. A tall matrix (m>nm>nm>n) has mmm rows in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn — dependent — so it is never right-invertible. Right-invertible matrices are square or wide.

Connection with Ax=bAx=bAx=b (AAA square or under-determined). Put x=Xbx=Xbx=Xb: A(Xb)=(AX)b=bA(Xb)=(AX)b=bA(Xb)=(AX)b=b. So a solution always exists for every bbb — at least one solution, and x=Xbx=Xbx=Xb is one of (possibly) many.

#10. The inverse, and special invertible matrices

Theorem / Key result: If AAA has both a left and a right inverse, they are unique and equal

If XA=IXA=IXA=I and AY=IAY=IAY=I then
X=XI=X(AY)=(XA)Y=IY=Y.X=XI=X(AY)=(XA)Y=IY=Y .X=XI=X(AY)=(XA)Y=IY=Y.
This common matrix is the inverse A−1A^{-1}A−1. AAA is then called invertible or nonsingular (necessarily square).

A=[−11−31−11222],A−1=14[2410−21−2−20].A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&1&-3\\1&-1&1\\2&2&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad A^{-1}=\frac14\begin{bmatrix}2&4&1\\0&-2&1\\-2&-2&0\end{bmatrix}.A=​−112​1−12​−312​​,A−1=41​​20−2​4−2−2​110​​.

Revision example: M=(2111)M=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}M=(21​11​), M−1=(1−1−12)M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}M−1=(1−1​−12​), y=(3,1)y=(3,1)y=(3,1) ⇒ x=M−1y=(2,−1)x=M^{-1}y=(2,-1)x=M−1y=(2,−1).

Theorem / Key result: Equivalent statements for a square matrix AAA
  1. AAA is left-invertible ⇔ 2. the columns of AAA are linearly independent ⇔ 3. AAA is right-invertible ⇔ 4. the rows of AAA are linearly independent ⇔ AAA is invertible ⇔ det⁡A≠0\det A\neq0detA=0 ⇔ Ax=0Ax=0Ax=0 only for x=0x=0x=0 ⇔ rank⁡A=n\operatorname{rank}A=nrankA=n.

(Diagram on slide p43: left-invertible ⇒(a) independent columns ⇒(b) right-invertible ⇒(a′) independent rows ⇒(b′) left-invertible.) So for a square matrix, a left inverse is automatically a right inverse (PSet 3 P12 b).

Properties: (A−1)−1=A(A^{-1})^{-1}=A(A−1)−1=A; (AB)−1=B−1A−1(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}(AB)−1=B−1A−1 (order reverses); (A⊤)−1=(A−1)⊤(A^\top)^{-1}=(A^{-1})^\top(A⊤)−1=(A−1)⊤; (αA)−1=α−1A−1(\alpha A)^{-1}=\alpha^{-1}A^{-1}(αA)−1=α−1A−1.

  • Identity: I−1=II^{-1}=II−1=I since II=III=III=I.
  • Diagonal: invertible iff all diagonal entries are non-zero, with diag⁡(A11,…,Ann)−1=diag⁡(A11−1,…,Ann−1)\operatorname{diag}(A_{11},\dots,A_{nn})^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(A_{11}^{-1},\dots,A_{nn}^{-1})diag(A11​,…,Ann​)−1=diag(A11−1​,…,Ann−1​) (multiply: each diagonal entry becomes Aii/Aii=1A_{ii}/A_{ii}=1Aii​/Aii​=1).
  • Vandermonde matrix A=[1t1t12⋯t1n−1⋮⋮1tntn2⋯tnn−1]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&t_1&t_1^2&\cdots&t_1^{n-1}\\ \vdots&&&&\vdots\\ 1&t_n&t_n^2&\cdots&t_n^{n-1}\end{bmatrix}A=​1⋮1​t1​tn​​t12​tn2​​⋯⋯​t1n−1​⋮tnn−1​​​: used for polynomial fitting (row iii evaluates 1,t,t2,…1,t,t^2,\dots1,t,t2,… at tit_iti​); invertible when the tit_iti​ are distinct (a degree-(n−1)(n-1)(n−1) polynomial vanishing at nnn distinct points must be zero).
  • Gram matrix A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A is nonsingular iff AAA has linearly independent columns.
Derivation: Gram matrix invertibility (slide p45, Tutorial 1)

Suppose AAA has independent columns and A⊤Ax=0A^\top Ax=0A⊤Ax=0. Multiply by x⊤x^\topx⊤:
0=x⊤A⊤Ax=(Ax)⊤(Ax)=∥Ax∥2 ⇒ Ax=0 ⇒ x=00=x^\top A^\top Ax=(Ax)^\top(Ax)=\|Ax\|^2\ \Rightarrow\ Ax=0\ \Rightarrow\ x=00=x⊤A⊤Ax=(Ax)⊤(Ax)=∥Ax∥2 ⇒ Ax=0 ⇒ x=0
(last step: independence). So A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A is invertible. If the columns are dependent (Tutorial 1 Set 1: a2=2a1a_2=2a_1a2​=2a1​), the last step fails: Ax=0Ax=0Ax=0 has a non-zero solution, which also solves A⊤Ax=0A^\top Ax=0A⊤Ax=0, so A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A is singular. Set 2 (a1=(1,2,1)a_1=(1,2,1)a1​=(1,2,1), a2=(0,1,1)a_2=(0,1,1)a2​=(0,1,1)) is independent ⇒ GGG invertible.

  • Matrix with orthonormal columns A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n: A⊤A=IA^\top A=IA⊤A=I (the Gram matrix of orthonormal vectors). If also square (n×nn\times nn×n) it is an orthogonal matrix: A⊤A=IA^\top A=IA⊤A=I, A−1=A⊤A^{-1}=A^\topA−1=A⊤, and A⊤A^\topA⊤ is orthogonal too (AA⊤=IAA^\top=IAA⊤=I). For a tall AAA with orthonormal columns, A⊤A=IA^\top A=IA⊤A=I but AA⊤≠IAA^\top\neq IAA⊤=I.
Theorem / Key result: Orthonormal columns preserve geometry

If A⊤A=IA^\top A=IA⊤A=I then for all x,yx,yx,y:
inner product (Ax)⊤(Ay)=x⊤A⊤Ay=x⊤y(Ax)^\top(Ay)=x^\top A^\top Ay=x^\top y(Ax)⊤(Ay)=x⊤A⊤Ay=x⊤y;
norm ∥Ax∥=((Ax)⊤(Ax))1/2=(x⊤x)1/2=∥x∥\|Ax\|=((Ax)^\top(Ax))^{1/2}=(x^\top x)^{1/2}=\|x\|∥Ax∥=((Ax)⊤(Ax))1/2=(x⊤x)1/2=∥x∥;
distance ∥Ax−Ay∥=∥A(x−y)∥=∥x−y∥\|Ax-Ay\|=\|A(x-y)\|=\|x-y\|∥Ax−Ay∥=∥A(x−y)∥=∥x−y∥;
angle ∠(Ax,Ay)=∠(x,y)\angle(Ax,Ay)=\angle(x,y)∠(Ax,Ay)=∠(x,y).
A linear map with orthonormal columns is a rigid motion (rotation/reflection).

Worked example: Proof questions (2024 Mid, Problem 3)

(a) Orthogonal QQQ: Q⊤Q=IQ^\top Q=IQ⊤Q=I; multiply on the right by Q−1Q^{-1}Q−1 ⇒ Q⊤=Q−1Q^\top=Q^{-1}Q⊤=Q−1. (b) ∥Qx∥2=x⊤Q⊤Qx=x⊤x\|Qx\|^2=x^\top Q^\top Qx=x^\top x∥Qx∥2=x⊤Q⊤Qx=x⊤x ⇒ norms (and similarly angles) preserved. 2025 Mid MCQ: Q⊤Q=IQ^\top Q=IQ⊤Q=I, Q−1=Q⊤Q^{-1}=Q^\topQ−1=Q⊤, ∥Qx∥2=∥x∥2\|Qx\|_2=\|x\|_2∥Qx∥2​=∥x∥2​ are all equivalent characterisations; "all eigenvalues positive" is not.
Rotation by 90∘90^\circ90∘: Q=(0−110)Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}Q=(01​−10​), Q⊤Q=IQ^\top Q=IQ⊤Q=I — never singular; its inverse (rotate back) is Q⊤Q^\topQ⊤.

Common trap: Singular matrices destroy information

M=(1224)M=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}M=(12​24​) (column 2 = 2 × column 1) sends x=(2,−1)x=(2,-1)x=(2,−1) to 000. Adding any multiple of (2,−1)(2,-1)(2,−1) to an input doesn't change the output, so the input cannot be recovered — no inverse can exist. If MMM is invertible and Mx=0Mx=0Mx=0 then x=M−10=0x=M^{-1}0=0x=M−10=0.
Computational caution (outline): in practice we do not form A−1A^{-1}A−1 explicitly to solve Ax=bAx=bAx=b — we solve the system directly (elimination/factorisation); explicit inversion is slower and less accurate, especially when AAA is ill-conditioned (nearly singular).

Remember

Square + independent columns ⇔ invertible ⇔ det⁡≠0\det\neq0det=0; then x=A−1bx=A^{-1}bx=A−1b is the unique solution; orthogonal matrices invert by transposing and preserve lengths and angles.

#11. Determinant and geometric transformations (outline & revision notes)

Definition: Determinant

A scalar det⁡(M)\det(M)det(M) for square MMM that measures how MMM scales area (2-D) or volume (n-D). For 2×22\times22×2: det⁡(abcd)=ad−bc\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=ad-bcdet(ac​bd​)=ad−bc. ∣det⁡M∣=2|\det M|=2∣detM∣=2 doubles areas; det⁡M=0\det M=0detM=0 collapses space onto a line/point (area 0) ⇒ singular; a negative determinant flips orientation.

Rules (used in Mid MCQs): MMM invertible ⇔ det⁡M≠0\det M\neq0detM=0; det⁡(AB)=det⁡Adet⁡B\det(AB)=\det A\det Bdet(AB)=detAdetB; det⁡(A⊤)=det⁡A\det(A^\top)=\det Adet(A⊤)=detA; det⁡(A−1)=1/det⁡A\det(A^{-1})=1/\det Adet(A−1)=1/detA; det⁡(cA)=cndet⁡A\det(cA)=c^n\det Adet(cA)=cndetA for A∈Rn×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}A∈Rn×n (so c2c^2c2 for 2×22\times22×2); triangular/diagonal ⇒ product of diagonal entries; det⁡A=∏iλi\det A=\prod_i\lambda_idetA=∏i​λi​ (L06).

Standard 2-D transformations x↦Mxx\mapsto Mxx↦Mx:

Transformation Matrix Effect det⁡\detdet
Rotation by θ\thetaθ (cos⁡θ−sin⁡θsin⁡θcos⁡θ)\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}(cosθsinθ​−sinθcosθ​) turns vectors, keeps lengths (orthogonal) 1
Scaling (s100s2)\begin{pmatrix}s_1&0\\0&s_2\end{pmatrix}(s1​0​0s2​​) stretches axes s1s2s_1s_2s1​s2​
Shear (1k01)\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}(10​k1​) slides xxx by k⋅yk\cdot yk⋅y 1

Remember

∣det⁡M∣|\det M|∣detM∣ is the area/volume scaling factor; det⁡=0\det=0det=0 means the map flattens space and cannot be undone.

#12. Pseudo-inverses

Definition: Left pseudo-inverse (tall or square AAA, independent columns)

If A∈Rm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}A∈Rm×n has linearly independent columns (so m≥nm\ge nm≥n), then A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A is invertible and
A†=(A⊤A)−1A⊤∈Rn×m,A†A=(A⊤A)−1(A⊤A)=I.A^\dagger=(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m},\qquad A^\dagger A=(A^\top A)^{-1}(A^\top A)=I .A†=(A⊤A)−1A⊤∈Rn×m,A†A=(A⊤A)−1(A⊤A)=I.
Equivalent statements: AAA is left-invertible ⇔ columns of AAA independent ⇔ A⊤AA^\top AA⊤A nonsingular.

Definition: Right pseudo-inverse (wide or square AAA, independent rows)

If AAA has linearly independent rows (m≤nm\le nm≤n), AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ is invertible and
A†=A⊤(AA⊤)−1,AA†=(AA⊤)(AA⊤)−1=I.A^\dagger=A^\top(AA^\top)^{-1},\qquad AA^\dagger=(AA^\top)(AA^\top)^{-1}=I .A†=A⊤(AA⊤)−1,AA†=(AA⊤)(AA⊤)−1=I.
Equivalent: AAA right-invertible ⇔ rows independent ⇔ AA⊤AA^\topAA⊤ nonsingular.

If AAA is square and invertible, both formulas reduce to A−1A^{-1}A−1.

Worked example: PSet 3, P11

A=(100111)A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}A=​101​011​​: A⊤A=(2112)A^\top A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}A⊤A=(21​12​), (A⊤A)−1=13(2−1−12)(A^\top A)^{-1}=\tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}(A⊤A)−1=31​(2−1​−12​),
A†=13(2−11−121),A†A=13(3003)=I2.A^\dagger=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&1\\-1&2&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad A^\dagger A=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}=I_2 .A†=31​(2−1​−12​11​),A†A=31​(30​03​)=I2​.

Why it matters in AI (developed in L05):

  • Tall case: when Ax=bAx=bAx=b has no exact solution, x⋆=A†b=(A⊤A)−1A⊤bx^\star=A^\dagger b=(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top bx⋆=A†b=(A⊤A)−1A⊤b minimises ∥Ax−b∥22\|Ax-b\|_2^2∥Ax−b∥22​ — the least-squares solution, i.e. ordinary linear regression (Quiz 4 d: "the pseudo-inverse can estimate xxx even when Ax=bAx=bAx=b has no exact solution" — True).
  • Wide case: among the infinitely many solutions, x⋆=A†bx^\star=A^\dagger bx⋆=A†b is the one with minimum norm ∥x∥2\|x\|_2∥x∥2​.
  • The general Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse A+A^+A+ exists for every matrix (any shape, any rank), equals A−1A^{-1}A−1 when that exists, and always satisfies AA+A=AAA^+A=AAA+A=A (2024 Mid MCQ 23).
  • If M∈R5×2M\in\mathbb{R}^{5\times2}M∈R5×2 has independent columns then M†∈R2×5M^\dagger\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times5}M†∈R2×5 and M†M=I2M^\dagger M=I_2M†M=I2​.

Remember

Tall + independent columns: A†=(A⊤A)−1A⊤A^\dagger=(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\topA†=(A⊤A)−1A⊤ (left inverse, least squares); wide + independent rows: A†=A⊤(AA⊤)−1A^\dagger=A^\top(AA^\top)^{-1}A†=A⊤(AA⊤)−1 (right inverse, minimum-norm solution).

Exam pattern: How this lecture has been examined
  • Quiz 3 (2026): symmetric + skew decomposition; AbAbAb as a combination of columns.
  • Quiz 4 (2026): T/F on left inverses of wide matrices, uniqueness with a left inverse, "more equations guarantees a solution", pseudo-inverse with no exact solution; classify systems; outer product and its rank; linear classifier scores.
  • Mids: dimension of matrix expressions; Frobenius norm MCQ; prove Q−1=Q⊤Q^{-1}=Q^\topQ−1=Q⊤ and norm preservation; left-inverse MCQs ("exists only with full row rank" — false; "used to solve over-determined systems" — true; "can be multiple" — true); det⁡\detdet rules; pseudo-inverse MCQs.
Remember: The one line for this lecture

A matrix is a linear map x↦Ax=∑jxjajx\mapsto Ax=\sum_jx_ja_jx↦Ax=∑j​xj​aj​; multiplying composes maps (sizes must chain, order matters, (AB)⊤=B⊤A⊤(AB)^\top=B^\top A^\top(AB)⊤=B⊤A⊤), and whether Ax=bAx=bAx=b can be undone is decided by independence of columns (left inverse, at most one solution) and of rows (right inverse, at least one solution) — both together give A−1A^{-1}A−1, and the pseudo-inverse (A⊤A)−1A⊤(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top(A⊤A)−1A⊤ handles the tall case by least squares.
